route_described: Route not given; Stein assumes 'one of the direct routes leading through Bunér' northwards. Direct map distance Und–Manglaur 57 miles (map, not road). With his rule (road = map + 1/4, + c.1/3 in difficult country) the road would be c.71–76 miles (my arithmetic; Stein does not state it).
stein_on_li: 600 li vs 57 map miles is 'easily accounted for by the natural difficulties of the track'; he contrasts it with the 200 li to Mahāvana to refute Mahāban (40 map miles).
quote: Referring now to the relative position of Und and Manglaur as fixed by modern surveys, we find that the capital of ancient Udydna lies almost exactly due north of Und and at a direct distance of 57 miles as measured on the map.

route_described: Same leg: Stein's explicit verdict on the 600 li.
stein_on_li: Excess of 600 li over the map distance explained by the difficult track (road-measure reading).
quote: The increased length of Hiuen Tsiang’s road measurement, 600 /, against the direct distance on the map, is in the light of the explanations given above easily accounted for by the natural difficulties of the track.

route_described: Stein paraphrases the 600 li as six marches across mountains and valleys (his rendering, i.e. 100 li per march; no route named).
stein_on_li: Implicitly reads 600 li as six day-marches.
quote: Hsuan-tsang started for Udyana northward from the city of Udabhanda or Und on the Indus and reached it after six marches across mountains and valleys

route_described: General rule Stein applies to all Udyāna/Bunér legs.
stein_on_li: Pilgrims' distances are estimates of road length, so in mountains always larger than map distance: at least +1/4, in difficult country nearer +1/3. Converts at Cunningham's 1 li = 1/6 mile.
quote: The examination of numerous cases, in which distances between well- known localities have thus been recorded in road-measure, shows that these measurements exceed by at least one-fourth, and in diffi- cult country more nearly by one-third, the direct distance calculat- ed on the maps.

route_described: Stein reads the 400 li as the devious pilgrim route Manglawar → Mahāvana (Panjkotai) → Mo-yü (Gumbatai) → Śivika stūpa (Girarai) in the Barandu valley → over/below the Karakar pass → Ilam. Sum of Stein's own stage figures: c.32.5 (26 map mi + 1/4, Stein 1898) + 6 + 10 + 13–14 = c.62 road miles (my sum of his stages).
stein_on_li: Direct reading of 400 li is 'certainly wrong'; 400 li = aggregate of the whole devious journey; Cunningham's 1/6-mile li makes the totals agree 'still more closely'.
quote: In this case the distance of 400 li would explain itself quite correctly as the aggregate for the whole journey from Manglawar to the sites in the Barandu valley and thence on to Ilam.

route_described: Last stage of Stein's reconstructed route: road Girarai → Ilam-sar.
stein_on_li: 13–14 road miles = 65–70 li (i.e. 5 li/mile); aggregate of all stage figures approaches 400 li.
quote: prom Girarai, -where I have located the last named site, to Ilam-sar the road distance cannot be reckoned at less -than 13 or 14 miles, corresponding to 65 or 70 U.

route_described: Stein on the stated distance taken as direct (the '500' is in the OCR/print; the text figure is 400 li; Stein 1898 p. 54 has '400 li, or approximately 66 miles').
stein_on_li: As a direct distance the figure is wrong; bearing (SW, not S) also less accurate than usual.
quote: The distance indicated from Meng-ck‘ieli-li or Manglawar, 500 li or approxi- mately 80 miles, is certainly wrong

route_described: Before his 1926 visit: Foucher's Ilam identification needs emending 400 to 100 li; decision left open.
stein_on_li: Notes the textual 400 li vs Foucher's conjectural emendation to 100 li.
quote: the versions so far known of the Hsi-y#-c/s's text put the distance at four hundred li, while M. Foucher must conjecturally emend it to ove hundred.

route_described: Nearest route Manglaur – Khalil Pass (W of Dosirri) – Gokand – Padshah – Elai – Panjkotai: 26 miles on the map; Stein adds 1/4 for road = 192 li (i.e. c.32.5 road miles). NB Stein's Mahāvana is c.26 map miles S of Manglaur, not the 11 km site now used.
stein_on_li: 26 map miles = 156 li at 6 li/mile; +1/4 for road = 192 li, 'as closely as we can reasonably expect' to 200 li. Against Mahāban: 40 map miles, ≥50 road miles = 300 li, not 200.
quote: It measures On the map about 26 miles, which distance converted according to the value previously indicated corresponds to about 156 Ji.

route_described: Continuation of the same computation (map + 1/4).
stein_on_li: 192 li computed vs 200 li recorded.
quote: to this distance on the map one-fourth in order to obtain the approximate road measurement, we arrive at the result of 192 di, This agrees as closely as we can reasonably expect withthe 200 /# of Hiuen Tsiang’s estimate.

route_described: Calibration (not in the requested list): descend NW from Panjkotai to Gumbatai, c.6 road miles.
stein_on_li: 6 miles = 36 li, the mean of the recorded 30 or 40 li.
quote: Its actual distance by road is about 6 miles, which corresponds to 36 /#, or the mean of the approxi- mate figures given by the pilgrim.

route_described: Calibration: Girarai–Tursak c.7 miles on the direct track marched, plus Tursak–Gumbatai; total 10 miles.
stein_on_li: 10 miles = exactly the 60 li recorded (6 li/mile).
quote: The total of these measurements is 10 miles, which represents exactly the 60 /¢ of Hiuen Tsiang’s estimate.

route_described: Calibration: Girarai – Banjir Pass – Swat River – left bank to Chakdara – Adinzai: 25 miles on the map along the route.
stein_on_li: 25 map miles along the route ≈ the map equivalent of 200 li (as for Manglaur–Mahāvana), so 200 li again = road distance.
quote: Measured along this route the total distance on the map from Girdrai to the central point of the Adinzai Valley above indicated amounts to 25 miles.

route_described: Calibration: road Manglawar–Shankardar c.13 miles.
stein_on_li: 13 road miles = 60–70 li, taking the li at about 1/5 mile, 'as usually applicable to Chinese road measurements in the Western regions'.
quote: The distance by road is about 13 miles, the equivalent of G0-70 li , taking the U at the value of about one-fifth of a mile, as usually applicable to Chinese road measurements in the ‘ Western regions.

route_described: Manglaur NE through the Ghorband/Kanda hills to the Indus at Besham, then up the Indus gorges (Indus Kohistan) to Darel. Route measured on the Northern Transfrontier sheets: c.140 miles; Stein says the real road must be at least 1/3 more (≥ c.187 miles, my arithmetic).
stein_on_li: Xuanzang's 1000+ li 'agrees well' with the sketch maps; map route length must be increased by at least one-third for the difficult ground. Possibly hearsay (Life), but from a trustworthy guide.
quote: Measured on the ‘Northern Tranofrontier’ sheets of the Survey of India the aggregate distance of the route from Manhitl, the chief place of Daré), along the Indus \o Beshin and thence via GhOrband to Manglaur amounts to about 140 miles.

route_described: Same footnote: correction to the map route length.
stein_on_li: Map route +≥1/3 for the exceptionally difficult ground.
quote: Considering the exceptionally difficult ground, it is cerlain that this must be increased by at least one-third in order (o arrive al an approximatcly correct estimate.

source: Stein, Innermost Asia i (1928), quoting Faxian
route_described: Faxian's descent from T'o-li (Darel) SW through the Indus gorges to Swat; Stein: the most direct route Darel–central Swat (Manglaur), same as Xuanzang's in reverse.
stein_on_li: Stein notes the Life implies Xuanzang only heard of Ta-li-lo and its road, though the Xiyu ji's graphic description suggests a visit.
quote: the  travellers  went  on  to  the  south-west  for  fifteen days  ’  through  the  gorges  of  the  Indus  until  they  arrived  in  Wu-ch'ang  or  Swat.

source: Stein (all on-disk Stein files, ASR annual reports)
route_described: No Stein route or distance found: searched Memoir, Buner report, MASI 42/43/37, Alexander's Track, Serindia, Innermost Asia, asr_annual (Ketas/Simhapura/Singhapura/Seng-ho).
Cunningham: Ketas 'not more than 85 miles' from Taxila (not stated whether road or map); 700 li = 117 miles 'certainly too great'.
stein_on_li: (Cunningham) 700 li too great by c.30 miles.
quote: Ketas is situated on the north side of the Salt Range, at 16 miles from Pind Dadan Khan, and 18 miles from Chakowal, but not more than 85 miles from Shah-dheri, or Taxila.

to: Kaśmīr via the Vitastā (Jhelum) valley, 'stone gate' at Baramula
source: Stein, Memoir on Ancient Geography of Kashmir (1899)
route_described: Stein's identification of the route: Hazara – Vitastā valley – Drang gate at Baramula – Huskapura (Uskur) first night – capital (Srinagar). Old road on the right bank: Abbottabad – Garhi Habibullah – Muzaffarabad – Baramula.
stein_on_li: No comment on the 1000 li.
quote: Hiuen Tsiang must have entered Kasmir by the valley of the Vitasta as he describes his route as leading to the south-east of Uraga, the present Hazara District.

from: between Mansahra and Abbottabad (old Uraśā capital)
route_described: First section of the Hazara–Kashmir route: Albiruni's 8 farsakh = c.39 miles, which Stein says matches modern route measurements from Muzaffarabad back to a point between Mansahra and Abbottabad.
quote: The distance of 8 farsakh corresponds according to Albéraini’s reckoning to about 39 English miles. Referring to the map and the modern route measurements! this distance carries us to a point between Mansahra and the next stage Abbottabad

route_described: Second section, up the right bank of the Jhelum: 84 road miles (Drew). With the previous row c.123 road miles from the Abbottabad/Mansahra area to Baramula (my sum; Stein does not add them, and the start is not Haripur).
marches_or_days: 6 marches (Drew, one very short); 5 marches Domel–Baramula on the modern left-bank road; Albiruni 5 days
quote: This estimate ngrees closely with the actual road distance between Muzaffarabad and Baramila which is given by Drew as 84 miles.

route_described: March counts for the same section.
quote: According to Drew’s table six marches are counted, but one of them is very short. On the modern route following the opposite side of the river five marches are now reckoned from Domél, opposite to Muzaffarabad, to Baramiila

route_described: Last section, on the left bank past Uskur (Albiruni: two more days).
quote: Two marches are still counted for this part of the journey.

route_described: Kalhana's six marches from the Uraśā capital to Bolyāsaka = modern six marches Buliasa–Abbottabad; Buliasa is c.3½ marches below Baramula (p. 85). Implied total Abbottabad–Baramula c.9½ marches, + 2 to Srinagar = c.11½ marches (my sum; Stein does not add them).
quote: six marches are reckoned from the capital of Uraéa to Bolydsaka, This agrees exactly with the present reckoning which also counts six marches from the vicinity of Buliisa to Abbottabad

route_described: Down the right bank of the Vitastā gorge from Baramula.
quote: after about three and a half marches we reach the side valley marked on the map as ‘ Peliasa,’

route_described: No road figure: converts 1000 li = 167 miles and uses it to place the Uraśā capital near Noshahra/Mangali.
quote: Its distance from Kashmir is stated at 1000 li, or 167 miles, which would place the capital somewhere in the neighbour- hood of Noshahra

route_described: Direct road Srinagar – Patan (half-way) – Baramula; no mileage given; Stein does not discuss the Mahāsāṃghika convent (W 140–150 li).
quote: Patan still lies on the direct road between Srinagar and Baraémila, reckoned at two daily marches

route_described: Stein: Xuanzang probably went by the Toṣamaidān route (Drang – Toṣamaidān plateau – pass >13,000 ft – Loharin or Gagri valley – Mandi – Tohi valley to Punch).
stein_on_li: No comment on 700 li.
quote: As the Tég#maidan route is the direct and most frequented route to that territory, it is very probable that Hiuen Tsiang also follow- edit.

to: Lohara (Loharin valley), on the Toṣamaidān route to Punch
route_described: Toṣamaidān road to Lohara only (Loharin lies on the way to Punch; Mandi is c.8 miles further down, then the Tohi valley to Punch): Albiruni's 56 'miles' ≈ 69 English miles, 'little in excess' of the actual road distance Stein estimated, so road < c.69 miles to Lohara.
quote: Albériini’s measurement accor- ding tothe previously stated valuation represents about 69 English ‘miles. This is but little in excess of the actual road distance vid the -Tdg?maidan Pass as estimated by me

route_described: Alternative winter route: Srinagar – Baramula – Uri (2 marches below Baramula on the left bank) – Haji Pir Pass (8500 ft) – Punch. No length.
quote: From Uri a convenient route leads over the easy Haji Pir Pass to Prants ov Parnotsa.

route_described: Cunningham: 75 miles on the map via Baramula and Uri, about 100 miles by road.
stein_on_li: (Cunningham) 700 li = 117 miles.
quote: Its   dis- tancefrom Kashmir, as measured on the map vid Barahmula and Uri is 75 miles, which is equal to about 100 miles of actual road distance.

route_described: No road length in Stein (Memoir only says Parṇotsa and Rājapurī were subject to Kashmir; route not described) or Cunningham (only converts 400 li = 67 miles). Searched Memoir (both OCRs) for Rajauri/Prunts/Punch/miles/marches.

Pir Panjal 'Imperial Road': Hurapor – Kamelankoth 7 mi – Aliabad Sarai c.4 mi – Pir Panjal Pass c.4½ mi (OCR '43') – Poshiana – Bahramgala – Ratan Pir – Rajauri. Miles given only for the Kashmir-side ascent (c.15½); no total.
quote: Ascending the valley of the Rembyar? or Ramanyatavi for about 7 miles we reach the point where the streams coming from the Pir Pautsal aud Ripri Passes unite.

route_described: No road length found. Stein Memoir mentions the salt road via Jehlam and Bhimbhar only; Cunningham gives no Rajaori–Taki route.
